speechtext:
I am most grateful for the opportunity to speak on this motion and I should like to congratulate the hon. member who moved it so early in the session when our memories are fresh with recollections of our recent experience.
I would agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), that there is an unanimous or near unanimous view, held not only by members of political parties but also by members of the public, that a shorter election campaign is desirable. I would also agree with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in their justifiable and proper concern with the problem of fishermen and other special categories of people who have a particular problem in registering their votes. However I think they may be mistaken in

thinking that this resolution provides the full solution to it, and I suggest that perhaps a permanent voters list is not the best way to go about solving the various components of the problem as they were outlined today. I have an alternate proposal to make and it is aimed directly at achieving the result which the motion seeks:
-so as to permit shortening the period of time between the issue of the writ of elections and the date the said writs are made returnable.
When the question of this permanent voters list was before the committee on privileges and elections, of which I was a member, so far as my recollection goes the decision not to proceed with a permanent voters list was a unanimous decision. I may be subject to correction on that, but before proceeding any further there is one other observation I should like to make concerning the special problems of special groups in the electorate. It has to do with the service vote. The service vote problem, which was given such wide attention in recent times, would not be solved by a permanent voters list.
In answer to another point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer when he was discussing the cost and when he suggested that other voters lists could be drawn from the same source, while that might appear to be the case at first glance, there would still be required a certain amount of processing because, as the hon. gentleman knows, there are different qualifications for different types of elections, federal, provincial and municipal qualifications, and there would be much activity related to finding the particular qualified people within a community with the right to vote in a particular election. While I can see his point in justifying the expense involved I do not believe such a list would provide a complete voters list for every electoral environment in the country.
The statement of the chief electoral officer to the committee, about which reference was made by the hon. member for Selkirk, was to the effect that the initial cost of establishing this voters list would be between $6 million and $7 million, and he suggested that it should be revised at least twice a year. I cannot recall whether it was during the committee proceedings, or as a result of private conversation afterwards, but I gained the very definite impression that in his judgment a revision four times a year would be the desirable arrangement.
I would be inclined to agree with him and other authorities from other jurisdictions who have expressed opinions on this, because of the problem which exists in the constituency of York-Scarborough where there was an increase of some 40,000 voters between 1958

and 1962. Forty thousand over a four-year period means 10,000 a year. If the list was revised twice a year, this would mean there would be 5,000 new voters going on the list at the time of revision; so that at any given six months period there would be an additional 5,000 people who presumably, theoretically, could be missed completely, to say nothing of the many thousands who move from one part of the vast area of metropolitan Toronto to another, or in and out of the constituency. I assume there would be the possibility that 7,000 people would be missed in York-Scarborough, or could be left off the voters list even if this permanent list were in effect. Perhaps that is, again, being too personal in connection with my own experience.
But if we wish to have two things guaranteed, as the hon. member for Skeena very rightly pointed out, if we want to guarantee the maximum opportunity on the part of voters to register their vote in our democratic society, then we have to address ourselves to the specific problems of dealing with specific groups, those people in hospitals and travelling salesmen. In 1960 we made quite an improvement to the act by extending the advanced poll opportunities to increased categories of people, but we did not come to grips with these other problems to which reference has been made.
However, I think we can resolve that in one way, by moving the advanced poll opportunity further away from polling day. There have been many cases in my own constituency when people were leaving the constituency for one reason or another, and the fact that it happened to be the Saturday before did not materially alter their opportunity to vote, because the trip they were taking was of such a length as to encompass both those dates. I think this is particularly true of people involved in such activities as fishing and activities which take them away for a certain period of time.
My proposal in the alternative, in order to provide the maximum opportunity to the maximum number of persons on the voters list, the maximum scrutiny of the authenticity of the people on this list, is to come at the problem from another direction; that is, to attempt to set down ground rules in an act in this parliament which would in effect have the active, public participating part of the campaign designated as being the last four weeks of the campaign.
When this suggestion was first put forward after the election, the Globe and Mail, in a very generous editorial, suggested that I was in fact suggesting bootleg politics. If this suggestion had been made when the house
Canada Elections Act
was in session there might have been a question of privilege here. However, part of the editorial reads:
-Mr. Frank McGee . . . will have public support for his proposal to shorten future campaigns. Mr. McGee is being impracticable, however, when he suggests that this can be achieved by a private bill-
The writer goes on to say:
This newspaper is sorry to doubt that there is any conceivable law that could compel a politician to keep his mouth shut for four weeks at any time, and certainly not in the period prior to an election.
I thought this was a rather whimsical view. But I do believe it is possible for the members of this parliament or some future parliament to lay down a set of ground rules similar in purpose, intent and operation to the ground rules that apply at the present time to the last period of the campaign. We certainly could have as a component of that bill an undertaking that no public advertising from a political party or a candidate would be allowed in the newspapers, on the radio or other public media. We could designate in that act that the post office would not accept mailing material or literature for distribution until four weeks before the beginning of the campaign.
I acknowledge at once that in this act one would have to permit parties to hold nominating conventions and to have meetings in various parts of the country. But this is very different from what I think we all understand as being a full-fledged election campaign with public meetings, public advertising, public rallies and the other accompanying factors. In other words, I think we as members of parliament have the ability to agree upon a frame of reference or a set of conditions which would in fact designate that the election campaign would begin at such and such a date and that any other public activity should not be engaged in prior to that period. I am not suggesting that politicians suddenly become dumb, in one sense of that word, during the first four weeks, as is suggested in this editorial; but I do believe a measure could be worked out which would in fact guarantee maximum participation, a thorough enumeration and a thorough revision of that enumeration; that we could add to the act special legislation to enable special cases, such as fishermen, service people and others to vote within that period. The service vote particularly poses the kind of problem that requires this longer period within which the election material could be brought forward in a way which would satisfy the specific complaints raised by hon. members who contributed to this debate.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the position taken during the committee regarding the price we would pay for

Canada Elections Act
this permanent list. That price is $20 million. The initial cost is $7 million, the running cost is $5 million a year, and assuming, as one has to in these things, an election every four years, we are adding a $20 million fixed cost which I suggest will not achieve all the objectives set out for it by those who support such a list. I suggest a counter proposal to save individuals and the public at large from this sustained activity and expense.
Mr. Speaker, I might just say a further word or two before I sit down. I think the campaign period reduced along the lines and subject to the conditions I have suggested might do something really effective in the area of reducing the cost of elections, the solution to which seems to have escaped not only this jurisdiction but jurisdictions in all parts of the world.

Mr. Speaker, as this is the first occasion upon which I have addressed this house in this parliament, I should like to offer my sincere congratulations to Your Honour upon your selection as Speaker. I hope and know that your presiding over our debates is welcomed by this house as a whole.
I am interested in the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for Selkirk, and I was much impressed by the contribution made by the hon. member for Red Deer. Unfortunately, since I was away from the chamber, I heard only part of the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for York-Scarborough. This is a subject which is of great importance to this parliament and to the country generally. I am very much in favour of the resolution. I, myself, feel that the most important result would be a lessening of election expenses, which was the chief point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer. I believe the cost of elections in Canada has become excessive and that the situation should receive the attention of this house. This is one occasion upon which that attention can be given. It is chiefly for this reason that I support the resolution. I believe there are occasions when private bills brought before the house by private members can play an important part in the life of Canada. The hon. member is to be commended for bringing forward his resolution at this time.

I, myself, felt reticent about speaking on the subject and I therefore had in mind listening at some length to various opinions by other hon. members with regard to the resolution before I made a contribution to the debate. At first I had in mind proposing that the resolution be amended so as to refer it to the standing committee on privileges and elections. Then I thought such a course might be disappointing to the hon. member in whose name this motion appears, because it might result in a considerable delay. But I was anxious that the subject should receive a thorough study. It seemed to me that on the face of it there was no compelling reason why the house should not pass the resolution. On the other hand, there might be aspects of the question which should receive our consideration. However, after thinking the matter over I decided I would not move the amendment but would support the resolution in the hope that it will receive the general support of the house.
The other principal matter which has been raised concerned provisions for the assistance of absentee voters and of voters in general who are called out of their constituencies and cannot vote on election day. The arguments in this respect did not impress me as much as the likelihood of lessening the expenses of elections. speechtext:
Crisis in Cuba
construction of bases for the launching of offensive weapons in the form of I.R.B.M.'s and that this constitutes a threat to most of the cities of North America including our major cities in Canada. The reason that I agreed to the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition was to ask Canadians as well as free men everywhere in the world not to panic at this time. This is a time for calmness. It is a time for the banishment of those things that sometimes separate us. Above all, it is a time when each of us must endeavour to do his part to assure the preservation of peace not only in this hemisphere but everywhere in the world. The existence of these bases or launching pads Is not defensive but offensive. The determination of Canadians will be that the United Nations should be charged at the earliest possible moment with this serious problem.
The President has stated that the matter will be brought before the security council at once, and whatever the reactions of the U.S.S.R. are to the statements made by President Kennedy, I think what people all over the world want tonight and will want is a full and complete understanding of what is taking place in Cuba. What can be done? Naturally, there has been little time to give consideration to positive action that might be taken. But I suggest that if there is a desire on the part of the U.S.S.R. to have the facts, if a group of nations, perhaps the eight nations comprising the unaligned members of the 18 nation disarmament committee, be given the opportunity of making an on-site inspection in Cuba to ascertain what the facts are, a major step forward would be taken.
This is the only suggestion I have at this moment; but it would provide an objective answer to what is going on in Cuba. As late as a week ago, the U.S.S.R. contended that its activities in Cuba were entirely of a defensive nature, and that the hundreds, if not thousands, of citizens of the U.S.S.R., mechanics, technicians and the like, were simply in Cuba for defensive purposes. As to the presence of these offensive weapons, the only sure way that the world can secure the facts would be through an independent inspection.
I should like to hear the views of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on this, and the leaders of the other parties, for in times like these the divisions between us always diminish. Any suggestion that can be made that will bring about an alleviation or a diminution of the obvious tensions that must grip men and women all over the world tonight, will be helpful. Our duty, as I see it, is not to fan the flames of fear but to do our part to bring about relief from the tensions, the great tensions, of the hour.

Canada has taken a strong stand throughout the years on behalf of peace. Canada knows the meaning of war. Canadians want peace, as do all free men in all parts of the world. My prayer this evening is that those who have the responsibility of statesmanship will always have in mind the need for doing everything that can be done to assure peace.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I think the house will be grateful to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for providing, as head of the government, an opportunity for a statement and for the statement itself. I am sure that anyone who listened to the president's broadcast must agree with the Prime Minister when he referred to it as a sombre, serious statement. It was only a short time ago that the president was able to reassure the people of his own country, and the people of other countries, that the action taken by the Soviet union in Cuba, while a cause for anxiety, was not to be interpreted at that time as the transformation of Cuba into an offensive base, which would have been a cause for even more anxiety. Therefore, when the President had to announce this evening that he was wrong in that surmise, that he had been misinformed and deceived, and that the information at his disposal now was to the effect that this island so close to the shores of the United States was being turned into an offensive nuclear missile base. That indeed was a shock not only to the citizens of the United States but to Canadians and to the citizens of every free country.
Surely the thing now, Mr. Speaker, is to prevent that shock from resulting in either a feeling of despair and helplessness on the one hand or panic on the other. I think we can take comfort, and the Prime Minister mentioned this, out of the fact that the President of the United States has properly indicated that this matter is going to be brought before the United Nations security council and the organization of American states. I think it is important, as the Prime Minister has indicated, that these international organizations should be used for the purpose of verifying what is going on. If that can be done, it will be a source of reassurance to all people in the world as to the seriousness of the situation and the necessity of doing something about it.
Perhaps it would be possible for Canada to take part in the discussions that will be held before the organization of American states because the president referred to them as western hemisphere discussions. While we are not a member of that organization, this would be a suitable occasion for Canada to participate in this particular meeting, if that can be

done. There will be no question about our participation in any appropriate discussion at the United Nations.
I can only add, Mr. Speaker, that in any steps the government of Canada can take, speaking for Canada, to prevent this situation from deteriorating into the indescribable horror of nuclear war, and in any role it is possible for the government to play, it will get the full support of every member on this side of the house. This, Mr. Speaker, is an occasion where we will be privileged to cooperate with the government in anything it can do, in any fight it can make, for peace and freedom in this crisis.

Mr. Speaker, in adding my word, I should like to express my own personal, as well as our group's gratefulness, for the frank statement by the Prime Minister tonight. As we have listened to the remarks of the President of the United States of America, our actions and our carryings on here this afternoon, have been put into insignificance, because certainly we do live in critical times. There is a sense of encouragement in noting the respect in which Canada is held by all freedom loving countries in the world, and that encouragement is confirmed again in the words of the Prime Minister tonight.
We have a moral obligation, not only to our own people but also to our neighbours and friends in this ideological struggle that encompasses the world today, and it is our obligation to make our own stand on these matters clearly understood.
During the last half hour I have been thinking a great deal about a statement which was made a year or two ago by a prime minister of one of the newer nations of the commonwealth. He made these remarks to Prime Minister Macmillan:
Events move so fast today, and on such a global scale that no man is any longer clever enough to calculate the expedient thing to do. Our only hope is to find and do what is right morally. Then events can never overtake us and we will find we have done the only thing which will outpace the immoral ideology of communism.
I believe it is characteristic of Canadians not to panic but thoughtfully and cautiously to watch the developments that are taking place with the definite conviction that it is our responsibility to do what is morally right and to make our actions in that regard known.
The situation about which the President of the United States spoke tonight is one of critical seriousness. We have seen it developing and, while we have not wanted to think it was as serious as it is, I believe the words of the Prime Minister have brought home the urgency of the matter. There may be a tendency to regard some of this as a result of 27507-3-52J
Crisis in Cuba
the political situation in the United States, but I do not think that is the issue that is involved here. Therefore I am sure it will be the wish and desire of everyone in this house to give full support to those entrusted with the responsibility of government in taking that stand which as Canadians we should.
I add to what the leader of the official opposition has said, that it is hopeful, in the face of the grimness of the remarks of the president, that he is willing and has already initiated action both with the United Nations and the organization of American states. I am sure our delegation to the United Nations is already assuming its responsibility in this regard and will be backed up by our thinking and our action here at home.
I hope we shall also be able to make our influence felt in the O.A.S. organization, even though we are not a member of it. This is an appropriate time for us to assure the member countries of this hemisphere that we intend to play our part in this matter. It is not only Cuba that is involved. The Berlin situation is serious. Probably the situation in the Himalayan mountains has been used as a convenient smoke screen for the situation in Cuba. We do not know this, but nevertheless it too represents a very serious situation.
On behalf of those of us in this corner of the house I assure our fellow members of the house as well as the members of the government, the Prime Minister and the Canadian people that we are most concerned and our fullest co-operation can be assured at this critical hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the atmosphere and the discussion on the speech of President Kennedy which has taken place during the last few minutes, it is rather hard for one to start dealing with the more or less mundane matters of finance once more. This should be an object lesson to a juvenile Minister of Finance who, when he spoke in the house in the past, always used an envelope for his notes. This time he was told he should prepare a text, and having prepared the text and having distributed it to the press gallery, he has now to go ahead with it. Otherwise he might sit down and call it a day.
However, in view of this discussion and the problems which are confronting us, perhaps it would be just as well for us to make a careful review of our own economic situation. Those problems may be difficult enough in peacetime, but we must also survey the future in what I hope will be a calm and dispassionate way.
Just before we moved back into the house to discuss certain matters, I was referring to the price level in this country and I would like to draw again to the committee's attention one or two factors in connection with it. We have been told that the exchange rate was going to affect the level of consumer prices very much. We have heard dire forebodings about great increases in prices, but I would like to point out that when we compare the level of consumer prices in Canada and the United States, since January 1961 the exchange value of the Canadian dollar has decreased by about 8 per cent but during that period consumer prices in the United States did not decline. They rose by 1.6 per cent and ours have only risen by 1.4 per cent; so that the decrease in the exchange value of the dollar, instead of resulting in a great increase in prices has not resulted in as great a price increase in this country as has been the situation in the United States.
Mr. Chairman, as I have said, I do not want to enter into any partisan area whatsoever tonight, but this I think should be said. It has been claimed that the measures introduced on June 24 would have an adverse effect on the level of economic activity of Canada. The facts up to date do not bear
IMr. Herridge.]
out these gloomy prognostications. Hon. members will recall that last April my predecessor forecast an increase in gross national product of 7 per cent over 1961. A review of this forecast has just been made in the light of recent developments. I can now predict, I think, as far as one can predict, with any certainty whatsoever, that the forecast will be met, if not surpassed.
Mr. Chairman, without any vainglorious boasting whatsoever, I simply say as a simple matter of fact and place it on the record from the figures which I put before the committee this afternoon and this evening, that the statements made by my colleagues and myself in recent months with respect to the economic situation of this country have been entirely justified and that we Canadians are living in the most prosperous year in Canada's history.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to suggest for one moment that all our problems are behind us. We continue to face a stubborn and deep-seated balance of payments problem which has been with us for many years. Indeed, since 1950 and even before we have faced this stubborn problem of balance of payments, and we are still facing it. It runs from $1 billion to $1.5 billion a year. These substantial figures are the measure of the excess of our imports of goods and services over our exports through these years. Financially the current account deficit has usually been met by large net imports of capital, and when earlier this year there was a reversal of the capital flow, the basic underlying problem came to the surface and we were faced with an exchange emergency.
There are strong reasons, Mr. Chairman, why it is of the utmost importance to this country to reduce and ultimately to eliminate the current account deficit in our balance of payments. First, there are real dangers in having to rely, as we have in years gone by, on the massive capital inflows which would be required to finance continuing large deficits in our international transactions. There was evidence last summer that such capital inflows may not always be available when needed.
Second, foreign capital import means an increase of interest and dividend payments to other countries. These payments already account for a large outflow each year. They can be covered either by an increase of our exports, a reduction of imports or further capital inflows. It would clearly be unhealthy for our economy to be getting further and further into debt abroad for the purpose of servicing old debts.
Third, large current account deficits can be harmful to the levels of production and

employment. In present circumstances, when our industries are not working at full capacity, such deficits on international account hinder the expansion of production and employment. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is very clear that we must work, and we must work hard, to achieve a steady reduction in this large excess of imports over exports and bring about a much better balance in our current international account.
There is no simple method of achieving this. It cannot be done overnight. We will continue to need net imports of capital for some time to come. We will always continue to welcome foreign capital and maintain a hospitable climate in Canada for foreign investors. Let me emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that the necessary basic improvement in our current account cannot be achieved by restrictive measures. Such measures as our import surcharges were essential in overcoming the immediate exchange emergency and will in large part have to be retained until there is clearly evidence of a basic improvement in our external financial position. But they cannot form part of any program for the lasting improvement of our current account position. Indeed, if they were retained too long they would defeat our purpose, for they would begin to make Canadian industry less competitive when it is clear that we must become more competitive. These are strictly temporary measures and we have already begun to relax them.
This country must adopt positive measures of a long term nature. These measures must have two basic objectives. First, they must put Canada in a position to export substantially more goods and services to other countries. Second, they must put Canada in a position to produce more of its own requirements on a fully competitive basis. Our approach to achieving more economic growth and solving the balance of payments problem is expansive, not restrictive. We believe that Canadians can compete successfully for markets at home and abroad, and we will help them in every way we can.
Last week our Prime Minister made public his letter to President Kennedy and the president's reply concerning the Prime Minister's proposal for a world trade conference of like-minded nations for the purpose of reducing trade barriers of all kinds. The discussion tonight has shoved to the background this proposal with respect to trade. But I would remind the committee of President Kennedy's enthusiastic endorsement of this proposal, which makes it clear that we have strong allies in carrying through this most constructive initiative. We intend to take full advantage of this opportunity, not only to find new and diversified outlets for
Ways and Means
our exports but also to promote stronger and more efficient industries in Canada.
When the government, last May, reduced and stabilized the value of our dollar, the double purpose was to promote economic expansion in Canada and to produce a higher level and better balance in our trade and payments. Canadian producers, competing in markets at home and abroad, now know where they stand. At the new rate, many who were on the margin before can now sell effectively, productively and profitably. The new exchange rate policy, which has been widely welcomed abroad as well as in Canada-I repeat that; it has been widely welcomed abroad-has laid a foundation for economic expansion. But on this foundation we must build. The speech from the throne spoke of the objective of more than a million additional jobs over five years. The speech also outlined a dozen or more measures to strengthen our economy and improve our balance of payments. May I remind the committee for a moment of some of the measures to which reference was made.
Trade promotion: Our program of trade fairs and trade missions is broader and more vigorous than ever and the leadership given by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in that field has been dynamic during this whole time. Export insurance: the house the other day passed a bill to double the funds which the government can commit to export credit insurance. Export of power: responding to changing circumstances, the government will now encourage long term contracts for the export of surplus power. Exports of oil and gas: under the national oil policy and in other ways the national energy board will continue to promote these exports. Application of science to industrial production: Canadian industry will be given additional incentives under one of the resolutions which I am reintroducing today. Productivity: the productivity council will continue and intensify its contribution to the competitive position of Canadian industry in markets at home and abroad. Technical and vocational training: this important program is growing even more rapidly than we anticipated, and when I refer in a moment or two to the financial picture which confronts us toward the end of this year the committee will fully understand what I have in mind.
Government administration: the revised estimates include many immediate government economies. The Glassco commission is making important proposals for improvement over the whole range of government administration. Agricultural development and rehabilitation: the agricultural rehabilitation and development program, ARDA, will be

Ways and Means
pressed forward. Then there are the wheat exports. Transportation: we propose to bring into this house legislation which will be implementing substantially the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation. This is one of the problems which has confronted this nation since confederation and which we believe the royal commission in its report has gone a long way toward solving. The taxation structure of this country has been built up-I will not say like Topsy, but on a basis which is not entirely logical. We have appointed a commission to deal with this problem but at the same time we have not limited the government taking such action in this field as it sees fit in dealing with the taxation structure of this country.
Perhaps the most important development of all is the national economic development board. The problems to be solved in the years ahead, if we are to create more than a million more jobs by 1967, are formidable. Moreover, we are not planning to put people to work digging post holes and filling them up again; the new jobs must be productive and competitive by international standards. Many of these jobs must be in the export industries; many others must be in industries replacing imports on a competitive basis. This is the road to a lasting solution of our present balance of payments problems. This is the road to diminished dependence on capital imports. As Minister of Finance with a special responsibility for the economic health of this land, I intend to take a close, continuing and active interest in this new body. In stimulating and guiding our economic development along productive. competitive lines, the new board will have three interrelated tasks.
First, it will provide a broad new bridge between government, on the one hand and, on the other, those who are thinking and planning the future of industry, labour, agriculture, and the other important economic groups in our community. It is an essential aspect of national interest to encourage and expand constructive thinking and planning about national economic development by leaders in business, in agriculture, in trade unions and in other major economic groups throughout the country. In a country such as Canada in which free enterprise is a major factor, business policies and trade union policies are as important, indeed, often more important and influential than government policies. Government policies are, of course, important but they are not necessarily dominant. The economic policies and attitudes of businessmen, of labour leaders, of farm organizations, will often have the greater effect on national economic growth. If government

and non-government leaders pool their ideas, if each gets to know and really understand the views of the others, and if, consequentially, the varied policies are effectively coordinated, we shall greatly improve the pattern, the quality and the rate of our economic growth.
The second task of the new board will be to supplement, develop, and expand our government machinery for economic analysis, particularly where that analysis throws light on our economic possibilities. For this purpose we want to make use of the best economic thinking that is available. I do not want to suggest that members of the government, or officials working for them, have not been concerned in the past with the probable course of economic developments. Far from it. But we are convinced that our thinking and planning can be improved if there is, in one centre, a group of trained people whose full time job it is to think forward and, may I say, to use a somewhat slang expression, to think big.
The third task of the new board, and by no means the least important, will be, in the
words of the speech from the throne, to recommend to the government: "particular projects or measures which it considers would be in the interest of national development, including projects which may require direct governmental participation by way of financial aid or otherwise." I lay particular stress on the projects requiring governmental aid or participation. The government, like everyone else, has limited resources. Government spending, and other forms of government aid, can be economic or uneconomic, can be productive or counter-productive. Unwise government spending simply adds to the burden of government debt and to the deadweight of taxation on imagination and enterprise. But, as the history of our country has shown, government expenditures of a productive character march together with and complement private economic expansion and initiative. Public enterprise and private enterprise can be partners if they work together for a single expansive purpose. I am sure that the study which this board may give to projects which come before it will result in co-operation of that kind.
Having covered generally some of the economic problems with which we are confronted today and with which we are likely to be confronted tomorrow, may I conclude by turning briefly to the situation concerning government accounts. This, of course, is of interest to the committee in view of the discussion we had this afternoon and which is likely to continue for the next day or so.

Last April my predecessor estimated that our budgetary expenditures in the current year would be $6,525 million. Since then, as indicated in the revised main estimates which I tabled last Thursday, we have arranged to reduce our requested appropriations for controllable expenditures by $228 million. On the other hand, there have been, or are likely to be, certain considerable increases in several of the statutory or contractual classes of expenditures. For example, the rapid and encouraging speed-up in provincial expenditures on vocational and technical training schools seems likely to increase our contributions to these projects by close to $100 million. The rising rates of provincial expenditures on hospital and other welfare services in respect of which we share about one half of the cost are likely to add some $30 million to $35 million to our outlays. The other evening, in another debate, someone charged the government with reducing its expenditure on the social services as a result of its alleged austerity program. When hon. members consider those two figures to which I have just referred, I think they will realize that criticism can be withdrawn.
Interest rates on our public borrowings moved up very sharply in May and June, and while they have moved down again quite substantially in recent weeks, they are still above the prevailing rates of last April. Moreover, in order to finance our improved exchange reserve position we have had to increase our total outstanding gross public debt. As a result of these factors the total interest payable on our public debt this year is likely to be about $40 million greater than seemed probable six months ago.
In other words, there is likely to be an increase of about $175 million in our statutory or contractual expenditures. Furthermore, it now seems probable that the year-end laps-ings in the various departmental appropriations will be rather less than we expected last April. Consequently, the decrease in actual expenditures of a controllable nature is likely to be about $200 million. This means our present estimate is that our total budgetary expenditures in the current fiscal year will be approximately $6,500 million. On the revenue side our largest increases will, of course, be coming from the temporary emergency import surcharges, and these will add about $130 million to our collections under the customs tariff. Current trends indicate that our receipts from other sources of revenue will be up by about $20 million. In other words, our total budgetary revenues for 1962-63 are now estimated to be about $5,930 million, or $150 million higher than our April forecast.
