speechtext:
With expected revenues of $5,930 million and expenditures of $6,500 million, my present estimate of the budgetary deficit for the current year is $570 million, or $175 million less than the $745 million forecast presented to the previous parliament, and some $220 million less than the actual deficit for 1961-62.
Excluding any inflows or outflows from the exchange reserve fund, which are quite unpredictable, our cash requirements for the current year will be considerably less than we estimated last April. Crown corporations such as central mortgage and housing, export credits and farm credits are likely to require about $125 million less cash advances than seemed probable six months ago, and-this will be of interest, Mr. Chairman-the prospects are that the unemployment insurance fund will need $40 million less than our earlier forecast. The reduction of $175 million in our estimated budgetary deficit will further reduce our cash requirements.
Our net cash requirements for the remainder of this fiscal year, again excluding the exchange fund, will be about $500 million. I hope, indeed I confidently expect, that we will get at least this amount from our net sales of Canada savings bonds, which are at the moment selling at a higher record than even before; although, of course, the period has not been long enough to work out a considered judgment with respect to that matter. We will, of course, have to put out very large refunding

Ways and Means
issues, since we have maturing market issues from now up to and including April 1 amounting to $1,165 million. This figure includes a government guaranteed C.N.R. issue of $250 million, but does not include $445 million of option bonds which holders are entitled to encash on April 1, 1963, but which they may and are likely to extend to April 1, 1976.
I am assuming now, Mr. Chairman, that the committee does not wish me to go ahead with the details of any specific resolution, the income tax resolution, which you, Mr. Chairman, or your predecessor in the chair, called earlier this afternoon. Therefore, at this time I will not attempt to give any detailed summary of that resolution or the others which are before us. All I can say is that we of the government believe that that resolution and the other resolutions which are included in the ones which we will be bringing before you will contribute substantially to the economic development of this country; that it is necessary that they be implemented at as early a date as possible, having been subjected to careful and full debate and consideration in the committee and the house, so that before the end of the year they can be brought into statutory form and the Department of National Revenue will be able to administer them accordingly. I will, of course, be very glad indeed, when the specific resolutions are before the house to give such explanations of them as may be necessary and to answer such questions and give such details as may be required; but at the moment I would think that this would be my general submission which I should like to make at this time to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by congratulating the minister on his delivery of a unique speech-a budget speech without a budget. Perhaps a magician or an old vaudeville hand might be able to get away with a trick of this kind at least at a children's party; but I think if I may say so, that some of us have been a little disappointed in what we have just listened to. Anyway it was short; but I am afraid I shall have to ask the indulgence of this committee in being a little longer, so as to fill in some of the gaps and some of the things the minister has left unsaid.
I was rather disappointed when the minister said that normally he was accustomed to speaking from notes on the back of an envelope. Expecting as we did a more full and complete review of the economic and financial problems which are facing this country at this time, and getting very little of that, may we suggest that in future the minister revert to his usual practice. As the minister must know, his remarks about the state of the economy were anything but complete. I can 
think only that this is so because of his embarrassment in presenting a budget without a budget speech.
I do not propose to discuss in any great detail the constitutional question involved in the government's failure to present a budget, but I hope that others may do this in the course of this debate. I do wish to point out, however, at the very beginning of my remarks, that any discussion of our country's economic ills and of the kind of action that is needed to cure them is made much more difficult by the absence of a genuine budget. Perhaps that is one of the reasons or one of the possible explanations for the minister's unwillingness to present one. One can assume only that the government does not want a full discussion of our economic ills because it has no effective action to offer for dealing with them.
He did what you suggested.

You had better wait until I am finished. The speech from the throne on September 27 stated this:
New budget measures will be introduced to provide further solutions to long term problems.
Three weeks later we are told that there is not going to be a budget for this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Who said so?

Well, the minister stated the other day that he thought anybody with any intelligence would be able to figure it out for himself. Mr. Chairman, this failure to present a budget can mean only one of two things: either that the government was completely cynical when the words I have quoted were included in the speech from the throne to be read by the Queen's representative in Canada; or the government is now afraid to produce a budget for the coming year. In either case it is quite clear that this government cannot be trusted.
Quite apart from the government's decision not to present a budget, the minister has failed to identify our long term problems and to say what remedies will be proposed to deal with them. It is quite true that in the course of his speech the minister read off a list of various proposals, but these various suggestions are not enough. They do not add up to a comprehensive program which will put this country in high gear again. This house spent last week in dealing with the Export Credits Insurance Act and the Farm Credit Act, and it is now expected to deal with certain resolutions held over from the budget presented to, but not adopted by, the last parliament. I do not say that any of these measures are not important, but no one would suggest that they are the main parts of the

kind of positive and all-embracing program needed to get Canada on her feet again.
It will not have gone unnoticed that the minister said practically nothing-I repeat practically nothing-on the subject of interest rates or credit, or on monetary policy. I find this most surprising in view of the vital importance of these matters and of their concern to all members of this house. It is true that in his speech to this house on October 9 the minister stated, as reported on page 336 of Hansard:
I do want to say right now that I deny categorically and absolutely that there is any policy of tight money in this country.
While I was astonished to hear the minister say this, I presumed that it was merely an example of his exuberance in his first speech as Minister of Finance; or perhaps he really thinks that money is not tight, incredible though that may seem. If so, I would suggest to the minister that he should consult with any of the small businessmen of this country or for that matter any of the larger ones, and they will tell him that if tight money means they cannot get bank credit at reasonable rates of interest for legitimate business purposes, then in Canada these days we have tight money with a vengeance. I expect that representatives of the chartered banks will confirm this if the minister cares to ask them. In the same speech, on pages 335 and 336 of Hansard, the minister stated:
As a matter of fact, I suppose I might say- I hope I will not be misunderstood in saying this as Minister of Finance-that if any of us can find any three people in any place in the country who agree on monetary theory, then we are accomplishing a miracle.
This is an amazing thing for any minister of finance to say, Mr. Chairman, especially one who follows in the footsteps of the present Minister of Justice, who referred to me before the dinner break. We know that in the past five years the previous minister of finance demonstrated on every possible occasion that he had no conception of monetary theory or of monetary policy. Surely we are not going to go through all that again.
Like your book, tell us about your book.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have been led to believe that the Minister of Finance received a very fair and reasonably uninterrupted hearing, and I think the financial critic of the opposition party should receive the same courtesy.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I was just about to say that I was intrigued by the minister's reference to three people.
I had not believed the rumours that the
Ways and Means
finance department was to be governed by a troika consisting of the minister, who was to be the front man, the previous or ex-minister, who was to make the offstage and offshore noises, and the Minister without Portfolio, who was to make the decisions and set the policies. The Minister without Portfolio is sometimes to be seen peering down upon us from the galleries. Today, Mr. Chairman, we have heard from the minister, we have heard from the ex-minister, and I think we are all sorry that we have not an opportunity in this house to hear from the third minister, the Minister without Portfolio. I can only add that I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that the troika principle would negate the usefulness of the United Nations and the same thing, I suggest, would be true of the Department of Finance.
I should like to say something now, Mr. Chairman, about Canada's basic problems in the economic field, all of which are interrelated.
What chapter is this?

Mr. Chairman, I suppose I should thank hon. members opposite for giving such a plug to certain publications I have written. My publisher told me at the end of last week that he would have to bring out another edition. I told the Minister of Labour that I was grateful to him for his contribution and if he had a claim to any of the royalties I should like to hear from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be a revised one, I hope.

Our basic economic problems can be discussed appropriately under four main headings, the rate of economic growth, the rate of investment, both public and private, our balance of payments, and the levels of employment.
First, let me speak about the rate of growth. The rate of production in Canada, after adjustments for changes in the price level, increased on the average by less than 2 per cent per annum during the years 1957 to 1961 inclusive. This rate was much too low. The population of Canada increased during that period, and when this is taken into account we find that the average output per capita actually declined in that period. This, I suggest, is a sorry record compared with what has been happening in other countries.
The other night on television the Prime Minister used some strange figures about our economic growth that bore no relation to the facts. I hope that the next time the Prime Minister or any of his colleagues plan to use the forecasts of the royal commission with which I was connected they will get

Ways and Means
some competent advice on the differences between an increase in real production and figures which reflect rising prices. Otherwise such comparisons are about as accurate-
As your book.
-as comparing apples and bananas. In this present year 1962 we have been in the upward phase of the business cycle and there has been some improvement in conditions. I think we all rejoice in that.
Why don't you smile?

But there are three hard facts that the minister did not mention and which I suggest should not be lost sight of. First, even in this relatively good year unemployment is averaging nearly 6 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis. Second, even this year's recovery is barely raising the level of real production and real income of each Canadian back to the levels reached in 1956. Third, most economists believe that the current business upswing is very near its peak. The year 1962 has been a relatively good one but 1963 will be another slow year.
Doom and gloom again.

We must expect a downturn in our economy with rising unemployment this winter unless the government takes the right action to offset it. I might say in passing that there is no sign of that necessary vigorous action from this government so far.
They do not know how.

My second point was the question of investment. Total investment in Canada more than doubled in the years 1947 to 1957 and prosperity during that period was high. In contrast, from 1957 to 1961 total investment, which includes government investment, declined by 13 per cent. Private investment declined by 19 per cent. Investment expenditures are the immediate cause of economic expansion and they also contribute greatly to increased personal expenditures. The decline in investment since 1957 has been a major source of weakness. It is the main cause of our stagnation and lack of growth. It follows from this that if we want to eliminate stagnation and to reinvigorate our economy the most immediate objective of economic policy should be to increase investment expenditures in Canada, public as well as private. I do wish to emphasize the importance of this.
My third point was our balance of payments, and I agree with much of what the minister had to say on this subject. We have had an adverse-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is gracious of you.

I did not always agree with the previous minister in what he had to say on this subject.
We have had an adverse balance of payments with other countries every year since 1952. In current dollars, this has averaged the sum of $735 million per annum in the first four years, 1953 to 1956, but in the next four years, 1957 to 1960, the average imbalance went up to $1,335 million a year.
Have you the figures for 1956?

Yes, 1 have. I was also going to give you the figure for 1961 to show that it was reduced in that year to just below a billion dollars. It was hoped that it would be lower again this year, but with the rise in volume of imports despite tariff surcharges, this hope may not be realized.
Now, those are the bare statistics, Mr. Chairman. What exactly do they mean? They mean that in the last five years our obligations for the goods and services we have bought from foreigners have exceeded their obligations for goods and services they have bought from us by the staggering sum of $6.25 billion. We have paid for this by selling off our natural resources and our Canadian owned companies and by going into debt to foreigners. Now, it is true that some professional economists do not think it matters who owns or controls Canadian resources and Canadian companies or who has the final say in the aftairs of some Canadian trade unions. I do not agree with this. To me, this non-resident control of our resources, this absentee ownership, has been increasing for far too long.
Since 1947.
However, it has been increasing especially quickly during the past five years.
What are you going to do about it?

If I am given a little time, I will be telling hon. gentlemen what this party will do about it. The foreign deficits that by 1956 were beginning to trouble Canada have since that time become bigger, and they have become chronic. These are the facts. Now, we know we have gained a great deal from the many new developments that would not have been possible without foreign capital, foreign know-how and assured markets for the materials that were produced by these new ventures. But we know also that when 60 per cent, and by now it may be two thirds, of the manufacturing industries of any country are controlled by non-residents, that country is facing trouble.

Now, I should like to give one example of the kind of trouble to which I refer. We have to expand our exports, including exports of manufactured goods. But our secondary manufacturers are not likely to be interested in doing this if it means competing in export markets with their foreign parent companies. This is one reason why it is so difficult for us to bring our international accounts into some kind of balance. The degree of absentee ownership that now exists is one of our country's basic problems. We should take steps without delay to reverse the present trends.
In saying this, I should like to add a word of caution. We should not take unfair or extreme action against people who, in good faith, have invested their money and their resources here. By doing so, they have helped us to develop our country faster than otherwise would have been possible. What we must do is reverse this present trend, but gradually and over a period of years. But we simply must get started.
Now, my fourth point under which I wish to discuss the economic trends and conditions with which we are trying to deal, is unemployment. Unemployment in Canada has averaged 6.8 per cent for the last four years. This was very much higher than it was at any time in the previous 12 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Are these d.b.s. figures?
Are these actual figures?
You do not like to hear them.
They are not actual figures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; if any hon. member wishes to ask the hon. member for Davenport a question he could ask him to yield the floor and the hon. member will deal with it.
I wonder if the hon. member will permit a question? The last figure he quoted on unemployment, that average, is that actual unemployment figures issued by the d.b.s.?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
They are not.

I am glad the Minister of Labour asked me that question because I wanted to refer to a recent study prepared by the United States government concerning rates of unemployment in various industrialized countries in 1960. It showed that the rate in Canada in 1960 was the highest of all industrialized countries in the western world. I would remind him that our rate was even higher in 1961. In referring to that study the other day in this house the Minister of Labour said that such comparisons between different countries were not accurate because the statistics were compiled in different countries
Ways and Means
in different ways. I happened to notice, Mr. Chairman, that the authors of the study said they had made an adjustment to eliminate such differences. I draw this to the attention of the minister.
All hon. members in this house will rejoice that this year unemployment has been running at a somewhat lower rate. In September, the number of unemployed was 48,000 people less than in the same month last year. It would be wonderful if there were any justification for hoping that the improving trend would be continued. Unfortunately and unhappily, this is not the case.
Gloom.

I have said on other occasions before I was elected to this house that these high rates of unemployment in Canada are a national disgrace. Translated into human terms, they mean misery, frustration and unhappiness for hundreds of thousands of men and women and the members of their families. They mean degradation and sometimes ruin for young people who cannot find work. They mean a sense of hopelessness for people over 40-and I happen to be one of them-who cannot get jobs in industry and are made to feel useless and unwanted.
High levels of unemployment are the result of low rates of economic growth in the last few years. We could have had higher rates of economic growth. We could have had higher rates of investment. We could have brought our transactions with other countries more nearly into balance. We did not do so because the government in power in Canada during the last five years was incompetent, and becau e of the incredibly wrong monetary, fiscal and exchange policies that that government pursued.
You don't believe that.
The people believe it and they showed it.

It is clear from the recent
legislation we have been asked to deal with, including the leftover budget resolutions that are before us, and the speech that the Minister of Finance made tonight, that the government has no comprehensive program for dealing with our country's long term problems.
In these circumstances I should like to review in some detail the kind of program that was proposed by the Leader of the Opposition on October 1. This is the kind of expansionist program that should be introduced without delay. It is the kind of positive program that would restore prosperity to Canada and result in the creation of hundreds of thousands of the jobs we need so badly.
The object of this program is to increase total investment in Canada, both public and

Ways and Means
private. In this way economic growth would be increased and full employment would be restored. These objectives can be achieved by conditions of easy money, adequate credit and credit facilities, and by fiscal incentives and careful planning. In the process the budget would be balanced out of rising incomes and there would be full employment.
(1)	The first essential of this program is an easy money policy. By this I mean much freer credit and lower interest rates instead of the tight money policy that is an integral part of the government's austerity program.
Monetary policy, as we understand it in Canada, began with the creation of the Bank of Canada in 1935. From then until the middle of 1957 the bank's interest rate varied between 1.5 per cent and 4 per cent. It averaged almost exactly 2 per cent over that whole period. Now, as we approach this coming winter, with the prospect of increasing unemployment, the bank rate is 5 per cent, and the minister sounded as though he were rather pleased with that.
The Bank of Canada rate is not in itself the full measure of interest rates, but it is the indicator of the impact of government policy upon the money supply and the cost of credit, and the figures are plain. This is a tight money government, a high interest rate government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Rubbish.

Despite the minister's protestations to the contrary and his associate minister's continued interruptions.
There must be some spread between interest rates in Canada and those in the United States; otherwise there would be a flight of capital from here but the spread in the rates prevailing in our two countries should be kept as low as possible and this does not seem to be the present policy.
Because of the importance I attach to this question of monetary policy I devoted most of my first speech as a new member to that subject. I shall not repeat what I said on October 4, but I do wish to emphasize that an easy money policy is of cardinal importance in the program I am putting forward. This being so, Mr. Chairman, there should be no possible misunderstanding respecting the government's responsibility for monetary policy.
Prior to the Coyne affair in June and July, 1961, when the present Minister of Justice lost his spurs-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They were left in the flanks of the Liberals.
Only a heel has spurs.
-and in the process his reputation-and if he provokes me I shall be tempted to bring up the name of Mitchell Sharp and what may happen to the minister one of these days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, how dreadful. Oh, dear, dear. If the hon. member has anything to say let him say it.
Watch your blood pressure.
Keep cool.
Mr. Chairman, I am a mild man-
And for a very good reason.

-but as I was saying, prior to that time the previous minister of finance used to protest long and vehemently, as was and still is his custom, that the government had no responsibility for monetary policy. When Mr. Rasminsky succeeded Mr. Coyne as the governor of the Bank of Canada he, and I am speaking of Mr. Rasminsky, issued a cautiously worded statement which in effect contradicted the position that the minister and the Prime Minister had previously taken in this parliament.
So did every other governor.

I do not wish to quibble about the language that was used in the statements issued by the governor and the minister, obviously it was intended to let the minister down as easily as possible. I do wish to emphasize however that in the kind of program I am proposing the government must assume full responsibility for monetary policy. The carrying out of that policy is the duty of the Bank of Canada. But the responsibility is the government's and there can be no room for misunderstanding about that.
(2)	The second point in this program is that in order to increase investment in the public sector of the economy the government should embark on a really extensive program of loans and grants to municipalities. They should apply to streets and sewers, bridges and sidewalks, schools and public transit services, and assist with the clearing of slums and building public housing projects. These kinds of projects should be looked upon as investments to be paid for over a period of years. Building them would improve our cities, towns and villages and in the process it would provide hundreds of thousands of new jobs.
The government's intention to cut down expenditures on public works as part of its austerity program is the wrong thing to do in

present circumstances. It will slow activity in the construction industry and thus add to the unemployment problem this coming winter.
(3)	As the third point in the program, it is clear that we cannot go on paying more to foreigners each year for goods and services than we receive from them for the things we sell to them. To do this would lead only to another exchange crisis and it would mean the continuance of the present problem of finding jobs for people who are unemployed. The right policy for Canada in these circumstances is to increase production in this country, wherever this can be done without increasing costs.
In discussing this question in parliament during the throne speech, the Leader of the Opposition mentioned the example of the automobile industry. As he pointed out, in 1961 we imported more than $300 million worth of automobile parts, which is the equivalent of somewhere between 40,000 and
50,000	jobs. As he also pointed out, certain countries in Europe have flourishing automobile industries although their domestic markets are no bigger than our own. They produce their own cars. Our automobile industry could do the same. This might involve some degree of standardization among the automobile companies of certain parts, including automatic transmissions. It might involve the implementation of some aspects of the report of the Bladen royal commission. Undoubtedly it would require full discussion with representatives of all sections of the industry. But if the importance of the action required was made clear, I am sure a satisfactory way of doing it would be found. Other examples could be mentioned of industries where we shall have to achieve a greater volume of Canadian output if our international accounts are to be balanced.
Mr. Chairman, we must strive for a greater production of Canadian oil. In 1961, last year, our imports of crude oil and petroleum products exceeded our exports by some $137 million and if natural gas is included in the calculations, and I do not believe it should, our adverse balance still exceeded $100 million.
Steps should be taken to bring our imports and exports of oil and petroleum products into balance. I know that some progress has been made in this direction, but a great deal more should be done, and it should be done quickly. Either we should increase our exports very considerably or we should take another serious, hard look at the case for an allCanadian oil pipe line from Alberta to Ontario and Quebec. This would be a dynamic way to encourage the oil industry in Alberta and
Ways and Means
Saskatchewan and it would also stimulate the construction industry and provide more jobs.
When water was the principal source of energy in Canada there were good arguments for prohibiting the export of hydroelectric power; but with the advent of other energy sources, including oil, natural gas and nuclear energy, this policy ceased to have validity. If we are prepared to export oil, natural gas and coal, then why not hydroelectric power, provided the long term interests and potential interests of Canadian consumers are protected? This issue was raised at the beginning of 1957 by the royal commission with which I had some connection. Being a new idea, it received a critical reception, especially from some of the hon. gentlemen opposite. But the Liberal party soon began to suggest that under appropriate conditions, and subject to the approval of the national energy board-which I seem to remember was recommended by the same royal commission-it would be reasonable to permit the export of hydroelectric power from Canada.
This course was bitterly opposed by the Conservative party, and especially by certain prominent cabinet ministers from British Columbia. But according to the speech from the throne, the government is now prepared to approve the export of hydroelectric power under certain conditions, and I for one am pleased that they have seen the light, even if the motive for doing so may be open to some question.
(4)	Mr. Chairman, I have given three examples-and there are many others, such as chemicals and petrochemicals-of how particular Canadian industries could be expanded and more jobs created. In doing this we must make sure that Canadians participate in the development of the industries in question. Ideally, these developments should be sponsored and financed by private interests, but if there proves to be an insufficiency of private capital for such purposes, then public capital should be made available.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not one of those who wishes to see the state compete with private industry. Our kind of economy works best in circumstances where responsibility for economic decision making is decentralized and in so far as possible is kept in private hands. However, it has been necessary in the past to invest some public capital in large undertakings and developments when sufficient private capital was not available. I think we should be perfectly willing to do the same thing again when it is necessary to get industrial developments going.
In order to achieve some of these objectives a separate department of the government should be established to deal with the problems of the secondary manufacturing

Ways and Means
industries. We have separate departments for agriculture, fisheries, mining and forestry, and they are all needed. The secondary manufacturing industries, that employ about one out of every five members of the work force, need similar attention.
(5)	Now for my fifth point, Mr. Chairman. There is too much absentee control of Canada's resources and Canadian corporations, as I said a few minutes ago; we must stop selling out to foreigners, even if they include some of our best friends and neighbours. The present trend must be reversed if we ourselves wish to control the economic destiny of Canada. With this as the objective it will be necessary to make a number of changes in our tax laws to discourage Canadians from selling Canadian resources and Canadian owned companies to foreigners, and at the same time to encourage foreigners and foreign corporations to sell their assets here back to Canadians.
As a first step it will be desirable to encourage such foreigners to take in Canadians as partners. But the ultimate objective must be to buy back Canadian resources and Canadian companies to the maximum possible extent. This is not a task that can be completed easily or quickly. We must first agree upon objectives and then work towards them gradually, but steadily, over a period of years. But we must get started.
(6)	Now the sixth point, Mr. Chairman. A regional approach is needed in dealing with our country's economic difficulties. We cannot hope to have a unified and vital nation if there are wide discrepancies in the degree of prosperity and levels of employment in different sections of the country. The Liberal program includes positive policies for lessening such inequalities by promoting economic development in the areas that are least prosperous at present. The principle is well established of providing incentives for new mining ventures in the form of tax abatements on profits for the first three years of operations. The same principle should be applied in offering inducements to business enterprises to establish new plants and other establishments in surplus labour areas.
(7)	The Liberal party is in favour of expanding Canada's export trade in every possible way. Tax incentives should be offered for increasing exports. We are against a restric-tionist trade policy and higher tariffs. We disagree with the tariff surcharges, that is, the across-the-board increase in tariffs, which is part of the government's austerity program. Raising tariffs will invite retaliation and this is already threatened in the case of United States imports of Canadian softwoods.

We believe that for the past two years Canada should have been working actively with the European common market. We do not wish to see the economy of Britain grow stagnant and decline as it may well do if she remains aloof from Europe. If this happens, we cannot hope that Canada's exports to Britain will increase. On the other hand, there are good prospects for increased Canadian exports to a prosperous and expanding European market which will include a growing and dynamic Britain.
(8)	If we are to prosper in the future, it will be imperative for management and labour to work together more harmoniously than they have done in the past. The recent reports of the national productivity council's special mission to Europe points out that such co-operation has worked to everyone's advantage in some European countries. It recommends that a serious attempt be made to achieve a similar result in Canada. This should be a prime objective of the government. My friend, the hon. member for Essex East, made an excellent speech on this subject just the other day. I hope we shall have the benefit of his views in the course of this debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How soon?
That is one we can count on.
Old faithful.

I seem to have struck a receptive note, Mr. Chairman.
(9)	As part of this program to put Canada in high gear-and I wish my hon. friend from Assiniboia was here this evening-we must make sure that our farm families have the opportunity to share fully in the national prosperity. That does not mean a lot of subsidies and handouts. It means aid to farmers to improve their production, processing and marketing. Such aid is needed not only on the individual farm but also by co-operatives and marketing boards.
How would you know.
I happen to be a farmer.
Wait till they hear it on Bay street.
Do you use a pitchfork?

If any of the hon. gentlemen opposite would like to come to Schomberg. Ontario, at any time, I will substantiate just what I have said. This aid involves programs for land use, farm credit and also long term credit for co-operatives; it means crop insurance, water conservation and the like- constructive measures for farm investment.
I believe that with the program I have outlined, with the kind of people who will

be needed to apply it, and with a restoration of public confidence we can resolve our basic long term problems. We can do something about the men and women who are unemployed and who want jobs so badly. We can increase the level of investment in Canada. We can bring our international transactions into line. And, with full employment, the domestic budget can be balanced once again.
If I did not believe these things, I would not have stood for parliament.
Having accomplished these primary objectives, we must go on to other things. We must improve the standards and quality of education at all levels, including technical training. We must see that all gifted students have a chance to go to university. We must do a better job in providing for our older citizens, including special housing as well as more adequate pensions. We must have a national program of health care, one that will work. And, above all, we must recapture the spirit that in the past has made us proud to be Canadians.
I do not believe these objectives can be achieved by the present Conservative government-a government that has lost the confidence of the people; a government without a program. We need a government which is not afraid of taking positive action; a government which knows what it would do. To get that kind of government, we shall have to have a new election. It cannot come too soon.
I should like to revert to what I said at the beginning of my speech about the government's refusal to present this new parliament with a proper budget for the current fiscal year. Let us consider what has happened since the previous minister of finance presented his budget on April 10, 1962.
1.	The parliament of that day was not given an opportunity to debate that budget. Instead, it was dissolved on April 18 and an election called.
2.	The Canadian dollar has been devalued and a fixed rate established.
In speaking of the use of the exchange fund in his budget speech on April 10, the minister of finance of that day said, as will be found on page 2697 of Hansard:
The government has not hesitated and will not hesitate in the future, to deploy a substantial volume of funds on one side of the market or the other in order to prevent sudden or erratic movement in our exchange rate.
A little later on in a discussion of Canada's relations with the international monetary fund, the minister went on to say-and I quote from pages 2697 and 2698 of Hansard:
Against such a background of general co-operation, Mr. Speaker, the house will understand why the fund, while naturally and properly retaining the ultimate objective of having Canada declare a
Ways and Means
fixed exchange rate, has not been disposed to press us into any hasty action which might prove to be premature and impossible to sustain.
We on our side wish the prospects of success to be more assured than they were when the Canadian government made its ill-starred attempts to maintain fixed rates during the years from 194S to 1950.
Only three weeks later on May 2, the same minister informed the Canadian public that the Canadian dollar had been devalued to 92J cents and the floating rate of exchange abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Are you against it?
Just three weeks later.

He and the Prime Minister then told us that this move had been planned all along. They seemed surprised when nobody believed them.
But to return to my list of some of the things that have happened since the April budget was presented:
3.	Since April 10 there has been an election in which the present government got only 37 per cent of the popular vote and a minority of the seats.
4.	There has been an exchange crisis of very serious proportions.
5.	The government has introduced an austerity program that includes the raising of tax revenues in the form of tariff surcharges which have not been approved by parliament and which, apparently, parliament is not going to be asked to approve.
6.	The government has completely changed the monetary policy it was pursuing prior to the election. Since June 25 credit has been drastically restricted and interest rates increased.
7.	The government has been accused of fraud in deceiving the public about the exchange crisis and the state of the economy-
By whom?

-and so far at least the government's defences against these charges have been anything but convincing.
8.	Important changes have been made in the expenditures that are proposed in the current fiscal year. These changes cannot be discussed intelligently except in the perspective of a complete budget for the year.
9.	The Prime Minister did not call the newly-elected parliament together as soon as possible after the election. Instead, he went off to London to represent Canada at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference, and there to express views with which a majority of Canadians do not agree.
10.	The government's popularity in the country has fallen sharply since the election on June 18, according to recent public opinion polls.

Ways and Means
11.	And finally, since parliament met September 27 it has been clearly demonstrated that this government's life hangs by a thread- if the temporary support it has received so far can be described in such a way.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You voted for us on the first vote.

Despite all these things the government and the Minister of Finance are now saying to this new house of Commons: "Get busy and pass the estimates for the year. Get busy and pass these old tax resolutions". The government seems to be saying, in effect, that this house includes a lot of new members, about 100 I believe, who should have never been elected. The government says in effect: "Keep quiet and do not ask questions about our financial affairs. We don't think you new members know what it is all about". The government says in effect: "Get busy and give us a blank cheque to run the country as we like". The government says in effect: "We won't give you a budget for the current year; what are you going to do about it?"
Under our parliamentary system, governments render a financial accounting once a year in the form of a budget. This includes the proposed expenditures, the estimated tax and other revenues, the amount of the estimated surplus or deficit for the year, the proposed tax changes, and the government's plans with respect to borrowing. It should also include a statement of the government's monetary and exchange policies. If parliament approves the budget statement that is presented to it and the changes in taxation which are proposed, it will support the government. If parliament does not approve the budget, the issue has to go to the people. This is the essence of our system. But if parliament is denied the right to examine a proper budget for the year, it might as well go home. Mr. Speaker that, in effect, seems to be what the government is saying to the hon. members of this committee, and I for one do not like it.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock?
No.
Keep going.
Read the last sentence again.

I will change the last sentence, Mr. Chairman, and say that neither I nor, I suspect, the majority of this house like it.
Now let us get the situation clear. In April the government presented a budget. It was a pretty free-spending budget with a large deficit. But the government would not allow the old parliament, the parliament that it dominated with so huge a majority, to debate the budget. Instead, it dissolved that parliament and put its case to the people. It tried to tell the voters that the state of the country was fine and that the budget was just right for it. Indeed if there was anything wrong it was that the government was not yet spending all it intended to. I say this because after the April budget ministers went across the country promising the addition of a causeway in the east, another trans-Canada highway in the west, and so on.
May I call it ten o'clock?
No.
